artwork.title: Rampin Head
artwork.imageCredit: Photo: Marie-Lan Nguyen, 2006, via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

lessons.title: Half in Paris, half in Athens

n1.text: A smiling young man with a short beard, and traces of red paint. Around 550 BC he was carved as a rider on his horse. Only his head is here.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Look low, at the base of his neck. There is a line there. Remember it.

q1.text: Where is the rest of the statue?

b1a.text: Yes. The Acropolis Museum in Athens has his marble body and horse. The Louvre shows its head on a plaster cast of them, and Athens shows them with a plaster copy of the head.

correction.tempting: Only a head sits in the case.
correction.truth: His marble body and horse are in the Acropolis Museum in Athens.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the Acropolis Museum.

b1c.text: Below the neck, this is plaster.

correction.tempting: The body under the head looks complete.
correction.truth: That body is a cast. The marble body and horse are in Athens.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the Acropolis Museum.

n2.text: The head was found in Athens in 1877, long before anyone matched it to the rider. In time it came to the Louvre.

correction.tempting: Many works carry their maker's name.
correction.truth: The sculptor is unknown. Scholars call him the Rampin Master, after this statue.

correction.tempting: A statue of a rider might carry his name.
correction.truth: The name comes from the collector who owned the head.
correction.evidence: The Acropolis Museum; Lechat (1900); the Louvre record.

b2c.text: Yes. Georges Rampin bought the head soon after it was found and left it to the Louvre. The name is modern.

n3.text: For decades nobody linked the head in Paris to the headless rider in Athens. Then, by 1936, the British archaeologist Humfry Payne did.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Head in Paris, body in Athens. How do you test a fit across two countries?

q3.text: How did Payne show head and body belonged together?

choices.label: He took the head to Athens

correction.truth: No inscription names the rider. Payne fitted a cast of the head to a cast of the neck.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Lemerle (1936); the British School at Athens (1936).

b3b.text: Yes. A cast of the Paris head fitted a cast of the neck of the rider in Athens.

correction.tempting: The two halves had to meet somehow.
correction.truth: He tested casts, and the Louvre still has the marble head.
correction.evidence: The British School at Athens (1936); Wagner (1997); the Louvre record.

n4.text: He is the earliest of the marble horsemen found on the Acropolis. Look at the wreath on his head.

q4.text: What does his wreath most probably mean?

correction.tempting: Kings wear things on their heads.
correction.truth: Most scholars read the wreath as a prize for winning a contest with horses.
correction.evidence: The Acropolis Museum; the British School at Athens (1936); Lemerle (1936).

correction.tempting: It looks like a pretty headband.
correction.truth: Most scholars read the wreath as a victor's prize, won in a contest with horses.
correction.evidence: The Acropolis Museum; the British School at Athens (1936); Lemerle (1936).

b4c.text: Most likely. Most scholars read the wreath as a victor's prize. Which games he won, and which plant the wreath shows, scholars still disagree.

q5.text: Where did the statue first stand?

b5a.text: Yes. The Louvre records the head as found on the Acropolis, and the body and horse were found there too, in pieces.

b5b.text: He may have won there; he stood in Athens.

correction.tempting: His wreath may come from the games.
correction.truth: The statue stood on the Acropolis of Athens, where its body and horse were found.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the Acropolis Museum; Lemerle (1936).

b5c.text: He only owned the head, much later.

correction.truth: The head was found in Athens in 1877 and bought by Rampin. The statue had stood on the Acropolis.

n6.text: One rider, two cities. His head is here in Room 170, on Floor −1 of the Denon wing; his body and horse are in Athens. Plaster casts join them in both museums.

n5.text: Statues like his were offerings, dedicated to the gods.

lessons.takeaway: The Louvre has only the head of this Athenian rider; his body and horse are in Athens, and plaster casts reunite them in both museums.
